title: Secondary Electron Plume Imaging and Applications for Mapping Electric Fields
content: Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) is a ubiquitous tool in materials research, finding routine usage in imaging the surfaces of samples with spatial resolutions of ∼ 1 nm, or even smaller for state-of-the-art tools. These microscopes work in principle by using a focused electron beam, with energies typically on the 1 – 30 keV scales, that scans over a surface, generating low energy secondary electrons (SEs) that are collected and quantified at each position to produce a micrograph. While this is sufficient for SEM imaging, there is a drawback in this approach in that information stored within the SEs, e.g. their energy distribution, which is related to surface potential, is not easily collected in routine SEM. Utilizing a set of electron optics and a two-dimensional electron detector screen composed of microchannel plates and a phosphor, we have been able to directly image SE distributions generated in an SEM, the so called ‘plume’, providing information on their momenta and energies [1]. Notably, this can be utilized to map electric fields based on the deflection of the SEs, even beyond depths accessible by other complementary techniques, as revealed through momentum-resolved imaging of planar p – n junctions [1] (Figure 1).
